pages.name: Two parts make the arrow
pages.text: Arrow `a` splits into two [[components]]: 3 across, then 4 up. Nose to tail they end at its tip, so together they are `a`. `i` and `j` are the unit vectors along the axes. So `a = 3i + 4j`. Wherever the tip goes, the dashed parts and the readout follow it.

pages.name: Write it with i and j
pages.task: This arrow, `b`, runs 4 across and 2 down. How do you write it with `i` and `j`?
pages.why: The across part goes with `i` and the up part with `j`. Down counts as minus, so `b = 4i − 2j`. As a column it is 4 above −2.

pages.name: A 20 N pull at 60°
pages.task: Finding the parts like this is called [[resolving]]. Resolve a 20 N pull at 60° above the x-axis. What is its across part?
pages.why: The 60° sits between the pull and the x-axis, so the across side is next to it. Next to the angle takes the cosine: `20 cos 60° = 10` N. The up part is `20 sin 60° = 17.32` N.

pages.name: Measured from north
pages.text: A [[bearing]] is measured clockwise from north, up the page. Bearings use three figures. This pull sits 30° above east. East is 090, so 30° back towards north is 060. The north part runs parallel to north, so it meets the arrow at the same 60°. North takes the cosine: `10 cos 60° = 5` N. For any bearing, east is size × sin and north is size × cos. The calculator gives the signs. Either way, only the angle and its labels move.

pages.name: 12 knots on 030
pages.task: A ship makes 12 knots on a bearing of 030. What is its east part?
pages.why: The 30° is measured from north, so it sits next to the north side. North takes the cosine: `12 cos 30° = 10.39` knots. East takes the sine: `12 sin 30° = 6` knots.
